steps.action: Reviewed earlier snow campaigns (CLPX, SnowEx, CMRES, NoSREx, JERBS, Tibetan L-band) and named the gap: none pairs dense, sub-weekly snow pit data with multi-frequency microwave observations over a full season.
steps.quote: however, with a relatively short temporal range, while dense temporal resolution is important to reveal the evolution of snow characteristics

steps.action: Designed an integrated fixed-site campaign covering a full snow season, from snow-free conditions to melt-off, combining L, K and Ka band radiometry with daily in situ snow, soil and atmosphere observations.
steps.quote: The experiment was designed to cover periods from snow-free conditions to eventual snow melt-off during 2015–2016.

steps.action: Sited the campaign in four neighbouring bare fields at the Altay National Reference Meteorological station for the 2015-2016 season and assumed snow, soil and weather conditions were the same across the fields.
steps.quote: it is reasonable to assume that the snow characteristics and soil and weather conditions are consistent among these four fields

steps.action: Built a 5 m platform with a 4 m orbit carrying the RPG-6CH-DP six-channel dual-polarized radiometer and calibrated it by sky tipping, reporting clear-sky sky brightness temperatures per band.
steps.quote: These radiometers were calibrated using the sky tipping calibrated technique with an accuracy of 1 K.

steps.action: Recorded brightness temperatures every minute at 50° incidence and ran 17 multi-angle scans after big snowfalls, every 5 d in stable periods, and more often during melt.
steps.quote: Multi-angle observations were conducted after every big snowfall, or every 5 d in the stable period.

steps.action: Checked footprint homogeneity by comparing brightness temperatures viewed to the left, middle and right of the orbit; they differed by less than 1 K, so the scene was treated as homogeneous.
steps.quote: the brightness temperatures observed to the left, middle, and right of the orbit varied within 1 K

steps.action: Dug a new snow pit each day and recorded natural layering, layer thickness, grain size and shape (microscope camera with a 0.5 mm ruler reference) and density (snow tube, shovel and fork); used automatic rather than pit snow temperatures.
steps.quote: In Field 1, a new snow pit was dug daily using a spade.

steps.action: Repeated every density measurement three times, added a fourth when a value was abnormal, and averaged the three.
steps.quote: In order to decrease the observation error, every measurement was repeated three times.

steps.action: Recorded four-component radiation (NR01) and layered snow temperatures (eight 109S sensors) every 10 min, and obtained hourly weather and soil data from the station's routine instruments.
steps.quote: the four-component radiation was automatically measured by a component net radiometer (NR01) manufactured by Hukseflux

steps.action: Consolidated the records into NetCDF files: removed abnormal values and filled gaps in the radiation and temperature series, averaged pit measurements, and supplied brightness temperatures and station data as is.
steps.quote: were first processed by the removal of abnormal values and gap fill

steps.action: Described the season's snow evolution: seven snowfall layers, grain growth with age and depth, shape metamorphism from rounded grains to depth hoar to melt forms, and a density pattern of increase, plateau, increase (Figures 7-9).
steps.quote: Grain sizes within all layers increased during the snow season, except in the bottom layer

steps.action: Compared density from the three instruments (Figure 9); the 24 % underestimate by the snow fork is taken from the authors' earlier work.
steps.quote: systematically underestimated snow density compared to snow tube and snow shovel by 24 %

steps.action: Described diurnal snow temperature ranges by depth and the evolution of soil temperature and moisture through the snow season (Figures 10-11).
steps.quote: The diurnal range of snow temperature decreased from top to bottom layers.

steps.action: Compared brightness temperature trends with co-observed snow depth, density and grain size, and attributed the post-4-January decline to grain growth; attributed the diurnal melt-period cycle to liquid water and refreezing (Figures 12-13).
steps.quote: Therefore, after 4 January, the decreasing brightness temperatures were mainly caused by the growing grain size.

steps.action: Compared ground-based brightness temperatures with AMSR-2 (18.7 and 36.5 GHz) and SMAP (1.4 GHz) at overpass times; temporal patterns and abrupt changes agreed, with correlations of 0.7 to 0.96.
steps.quote: The correlation coefficients at both polarizations were approximately 0.96, 0.7, and 0.88 for 36.5, 18.7, and 1.4 GHz, respectively.

steps.action: Attributed the large absolute differences from the satellites to the different fields of view, without testing this.
steps.quote: The difference between ground-based and satellite observations might be attributed to the different fields of view.

steps.action: Described the four-component radiation: the ratio of upward to downward short-wave radiation fell from about 95 % after the first snowfall to about 25 % on the snow-off day (Figure 15).
steps.quote: From the first snowfall by the end of January, the ratios between upward and downward short-wave radiation were approximately 95 %.

steps.action: Cited the authors' earlier use of these pit and brightness temperature data to evaluate and update a microwave emission model of snowpack.
steps.quote: The snow pit data and microwave brightness temperatures have proven to be useful for evaluating and updating a microwave emission transfer model of snowpack

steps.action: Concluded that grain size, not snow depth or SWE, dominated brightness temperature variation, and inferred a temporal offset in passive-microwave snow depth retrievals.
steps.quote: the dominant control for the variation of brightness temperature was the variation of grain size and not snow depth or SWE

steps.action: Compared the observed polarization differences at 18.7 and 36.5 GHz (increasing and decreasing) with the earlier simulation results and found a mismatch.
steps.quote: This phenomenon was different from the simulation results (Dai et al., 2022).

steps.action: Proposed environmental, snow and soil conditions as candidate causes of the polarization mismatch, and noted that missing subsurface soil moisture prevents estimating ground emissivity.
steps.quote: [...] behaviors at 18.7 and 36.5 GHz might be related to the environmental conditions, snow characteristics, and soil conditions.

steps.action: Stated the uncertainties (no subsurface soil moisture, L band only from 30 January, subjective grain selection, snow fork affected by wet snow, a single season) and recommended a small shovel or cutter in future campaigns.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is suggested to use a small-sized snow shovel or cutter to observe layered snow density in future experiments.

steps.action: Kept the claim that the released dataset is unique and usable for validating emission, snow-process and albedo models.
steps.quote: The dataset is unique in providing microwave brightness temperatures and coincident daily snow pit data over a full snow season at a fixed site.

end.claim: The IMCS dataset provides a unique full-season, fixed-site record of daily snow pit data with coincident L, K and Ka band brightness temperatures, radiation and meteorological data, with instrument precision and calibration stated, for evaluating models.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the daily snow pit observations made beside the continuously running radiometer, the dataset's claimed uniqueness would not exist.

gates.evidence: Acquisition was driven by a data gap (§1 ¶1-¶3), not by a stated hypothesis. The dataset faced one check it could have failed: agreement with AMSR-2/SMAP (§4.3 ¶3), plus footprint homogeneity (§2.2.1 ¶3). The grain-size attribution (§4.3 ¶1, §5.1 ¶2) rests on co-varying trends, with no test. The measurement protocol was set in advance (multi-angle schedule §2.2.1 ¶3; pit rules §2.2.2), but no hypothesis, analysis or threshold was fixed before the data were seen.

Internal Dicke switch calibration of the radiometer

novelty_claims.quote: [...] the best of our knowledge, our dataset is unique in providing continuous daily snow pit data and coincident microwave brightness temperatures
our dataset is unique in providing continuous daily snow pit observations over a full snow season at a fixed site
The dataset also fills the snow observation gap in mid-low snow-depth areas with a relatively short snow-cover duration.
The dataset is unique in providing microwave brightness temperatures and coincident daily snow pit data over a full snow season at a fixed site.
These data provide a new opportunity to analyze the difference between the influence of grain size on microwave and optical radiation

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, although the paper was reviewed by four referees (Review statement, p. 3529), so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims sit at lower statuses: - Grain size, not depth or SWE, as the dominant control of brightness temperature (§5.1 ¶2): best_explanation. It rests on co-varying trends, not a test. - The seasonal evolution patterns (grain growth, density increase-plateau-increase; §4.1, §7 ¶2): regularity_in_range, for one season at one site only. - The snow fork's 24 % underestimate: inherited from Dai et al. (2022), not quantified here. Internal inconsistencies, my reading: - The text cites ' [...] Fig. 8, snow density became stable after 15 January', but Fig. 8 shows grain size and density is in Fig. 9. Density stability after 15 January is used to explain a decline from 4 January. - Fresh-snow density of '0.05–1.0 g cm-3' is implausible (likely a typo). - The largest axes are given as 'up to 6 and 4 cm' while Fig. 8 plots mm, and 'short axes is approximately 0.7 % of the length of long axes' conflicts with those values. - 18.6 versus 18.7 GHz appear in different places. - The multi-angle date list repeats '3' in January. Processing gaps: the criteria for removing abnormal values and filling gaps (§3 ¶2) are not given, and the brightness temperatures are released 'as is' with no quality flags described. The satellite comparison reports only correlations and qualitative differences, with no bias or RMSE, and its explanation by field of view is untested (coded P). Composition: capability_first is the closest fit, but a stated data gap (Q) precedes the capability, and rivals appear only in the Discussion. This is inference. The grain-size attribution and the polarization mismatch with simulation are left without a test. Representativeness of one season is acknowledged as needing further analysis (§5.2 ¶3).

disagreements.target: CLPX, SnowEx and the northern Canada mobile radiometry campaigns (Cline et al., 2003; Brucker et al., 2017; Derksen et al., [...]
disagreements.support: The paper argues these campaigns were representative across sites but too short and too sparse in time to resolve snow evolution, and summarizes this in Table 1.
disagreements.quote: however, with a relatively short temporal range, while dense temporal resolution is important to reveal the evolution of snow characteristics

disagreements.target: NoSREx (Lemmetyinen et al., 2016) and JERBS (Aoki et al., 2003) fixed-site experiments
disagreements.support: The paper notes these campaigns sampled snow pits only weekly or every 3-4 d, and argues that sub-weekly processes may be missed.
disagreements.quote: Weekly observations could reflect the general evolution process of snow characteristics, but might miss some key details that occur at sub-weekly scales.

disagreements.target: Tibetan Plateau long-term L-band radiometry (Zheng et al., 2019, 2021; Zhang et al., 2021)
disagreements.support: The paper notes that this record has no snow pits and uses only the L band, which is insensitive to snowpack.
disagreements.quote: no snow pit was measured and the microwave radiometry observation was only performed at L band, which is insensitive to snowpack.

disagreements.target: AMSR-2 and SMAP satellite brightness temperatures
disagreements.support: Overpass-time comparison shows the same temporal patterns but large absolute differences and a weaker decrease in the satellite data, attributed tentatively to field of view.
disagreements.quote: [...] temperatures presented less of a decrease trend than ground-based observations.

disagreements.target: Snow depth derived from passive microwave remote-sensing datasets
disagreements.support: Because grain growth rather than depth drove the brightness temperature decline, the paper infers that microwave-retrieved snow depth lags in situ depth; no retrieval was tested.
disagreements.quote: the daily snow depth variations derived from passive microwave remote-sensing datasets tend to exhibit a temporal offset from those of in situ observations

disagreements.target: Microwave emission simulation results of Dai et al. (2022)
disagreements.support: The observed polarization differences at 18.7 GHz (increasing) and 36.5 GHz (decreasing) differ from the simulations; candidate causes are named but not tested.
disagreements.quote: This phenomenon was different from the simulation results (Dai et al., 2022).
